periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Story Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the story title and the central character Chinna, asking students what they know about goats and bells to build anticipation. Students look at the opening illustration in the textbook.

The teacher reads the full story 'The Tinkling Bells' (Textbook pp.9–13) aloud with expression, pausing briefly at key moments — Chinna's dejection, Kamala's advice, and the honest return of the money — to let students absorb the narrative.
Students follow along as the teacher models a second read-aloud of pp.9–13 with shared participation; the class echoes selected sentences and reads aloud the dialogue lines together.
The teacher invites two or three students to share, in their own words, what happened to Chinna in the story. The class discusses the title — why are the bells important to Chinna?

periods.teacher_notes: The story carries straightforward vocabulary but students may need help with words like 'dejected' and 'delighted' — pause and demonstrate meaning through gesture when reading these aloud. Ensure every student has the textbook open and is following the text during the shared echo-reading phase.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.14): answer four short questions about Chinna's story.

time_bands.activity: Having heard and read the story of Chinna and the tinkling bells, the teacher briefly recaps the narrative arc — Chinna's wish, his loss, the market trip, the honest return, and the reward. Students recall events in order orally.
The teacher guides the class through 'Let us Think — A.' (p.14): reading each question aloud, giving students a quiet moment to think, then discussing the answer together before students write.
Students write their own answers to the four questions in their notebooks; the teacher circulates, prompting students who write only a fragment to extend into a complete sentence.
Two or three students share their answers aloud; the class discusses whether each answer captures the story's key moment, and the teacher affirms or gently corrects.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 4 — how Chinna managed to buy the bells in the end — requires students to connect several story events; model how to link Kamala's promise, the returned money, and Chacha's shop if students respond with only one fact. The question bank covers four distinct events in the story, so ensure each question receives a genuinely different answer.

periods.activity_title: True or False: Checking Story Details

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.14): write T or F for five statements about the story.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads five statements from 'Let us Think — B.' (p.14) aloud, one at a time, asking students to raise a hand if they think the statement is true. This quick oral poll surfaces misconceptions before the written task.

Students re-read the relevant portions of the story (pp.9–13) independently or in pairs to verify each statement, then write T or F in their notebooks with a one-sentence reason for each false answer.

The teacher discusses each statement in turn: for false statements (e.g., the bells were not for Chinna's bicycle; the extra change was ten rupees, not twenty), students cite the exact passage that contradicts it.

The teacher draws out the moral dimension: the false statement that Chinna kept the money is directly contradicted by his honest action. Students articulate in one sentence why Chinna's decision matters in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse the amount of extra change (ten rupees, not twenty) and Chinna's intention for the bells (his pet goat Tara, not his bicycle) — the false statements in this task are designed around exactly these details, so a careful re-read of pp.11–13 is essential before writing. Encourage students to point to the line in the text that proves a statement false.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss: Why Did Chinna Return the Money?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — C. (p.14): discuss two moral-reasoning prompts about Chinna's honesty.

time_bands.activity: The teacher retells the moment at the pineapple stall — the extra ten rupees, Chinna's whisper, and Kamala's firm response — to anchor the discussion. Students are asked to hold that moment in mind.

Students discuss in pairs: 'Why do you think Chinna decided to return the money instead of keeping it?' The teacher circulates, prompting with 'What did Kamala say?' or 'How did Chinna feel when he lost his own money?' to deepen reasoning.

The second prompt — recalling a personal time when they found something that did not belong to them — is shared in pairs first, then two or three students share with the class. The teacher acknowledges varied responses and connects each to the story's theme of empathy.
The class draws together both prompts: the teacher asks 'What did Chinna's mother help him understand?' Students respond orally in one or two sentences, articulating the empathy-honesty link.

periods.teacher_notes: The second prompt invites personal experience sharing, which may reveal sensitive situations; accept all responses warmly and keep the focus on the feeling rather than judging the choice. Students who struggle with the first prompt can be redirected to Kamala's words about how Chinna felt when he lost his own money — this is the emotional hinge of his decision.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.18): listen to the story and number six sentences in story order.

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes or directs students to the six sentences on p.18. Students read them silently, and the teacher asks: 'Before listening, can you guess which event happened first?' Students share a prediction.

The teacher reads aloud the full story 'The Tinkling Bells' (p.18 transcript) at a measured pace with clear expression — this is the first of three read-aloud passes. Students listen with pencils down.

The teacher reads the story aloud a second and third time; students may now make light pencil notes. After the third reading, students number the six sentences in the correct story order in their notebooks.

The teacher reveals the correct sequence by reading each event in order and asking the class to confirm: students call out 'Yes' or 'No' and correct any mismatch. Discussion focuses on why certain events must precede others logically.
Students review their own numbering and correct any errors. The teacher notes that listening carefully for order — the story's sequence of cause and effect — is a skill they have practised today.

periods.teacher_notes: The correct sequence is: (1) Chinna wanted to buy bells for his pet at Chacha's shop; (2) Chinna discovered his money was missing and felt sad; (3) Chinna hugged his mother and told her about the missing money; (4) Chinna bought the tinkling bells after getting money from his mother; (5) Chinna went to the market with his mother; (6) Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller. Students commonly swap events 4 and 5 — Chinna went to the market before buying the bells, and the return of money happens in the market before the shop visit closes the story; draw attention to this during discussion.

periods.activity_title: Moral Dilemmas: What Would You Do?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (pp.18–19): discuss four real-life honesty dilemmas in guided conversation.

time_bands.activity: Having discussed Chinna's dilemma in the story, the teacher introduces four new situations from pp.18–19 and explains that each one involves a similar moral choice. Students read the four situations silently.

The class discusses situations 1 and 2 in small groups of three or four; the teacher rotates among groups, asking 'What would happen next if you did that?' and 'How would your friend feel?' to push reasoning beyond the surface answer.

The class discusses situations 3 and 4 in groups; the teacher picks one group per situation to share their conclusion with the class. The teacher invites agreement or alternative views from other groups.

The teacher leads a brief whole-class wrap-up: 'What is the common thread in all four situations?' Students articulate that honesty, empathy, and fairness guide the right choice — connecting each dilemma back to Chinna's experience in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Situations 2 and 3 involve peer pressure and loyalty, which may generate strong disagreement; allow differing views but guide students toward the idea that honesty, while sometimes uncomfortable, is the story's consistent value. Situation 4 about sharing a snack may generate lighter discussion — use it to close the activity on a warm, inclusive note.

periods.activity_title: Word Search: Values in the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.15): find ten value-related words in the word search grid.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the ten target words aloud — CALM, HONEST, LOVE, RESPECT, COURAGE, LOYAL, TRUTH, FAIR, KIND, PEACE — and asks students which of these words describe Chinna's actions in the story. Students give brief oral reasons for two or three words.

Students work individually on the word search grid (p.15), circling each of the ten words. The teacher circulates to assist students who are searching only horizontally; a quick tip to look vertically and diagonally is offered to those who have found fewer than three words.

The teacher reveals each word's location in the grid one at a time; students confirm or correct their own grids. For each word found, one student uses it in an oral sentence about the story or their own life.
The teacher asks students to choose one value word from the ten that best describes Kamala's lesson to Chinna and share it with a partner. A few pairs share their choice with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The word search grid (p.15) is 12×12 and some words run diagonally or in reverse — warn students of this before they begin to avoid frustration. The closing oral sentence activity is a light bridge between word recognition and contextual use.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.16–17): fill in blanks with -er or -est comparative forms.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens the textbook to p.16 and walks through the three illustrations showing Chinna, Charu, and Jasmine — tall, taller, tallest — discussing what changes each time a new person is added to the comparison. Students articulate the pattern before reading the grammar rule box.

The teacher reads the grammar rule box aloud (p.16) and writes three example sentences on the board using words from the story: 'Tara is small. Tara is smaller than a cow. Tara is the smallest animal on the farm.' Students copy and underline the suffix.

Students complete the five fill-in blanks in 'Let us Learn — B.' (p.17) individually. The teacher circulates and draws attention to students who add -er to a superlative context or vice versa — asking 'Is this comparing two or more than two?' as a self-check prompt.

The teacher reviews the answers aloud; for each blank, a student reads the completed sentence and identifies whether the comparison is between two things (-er) or within a whole group (-est). The teacher affirms correct reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error at this level is using 'tallest than' or dropping 'the' before superlatives — the grammar rule box on p.16 addresses both; draw students' attention to 'the' explicitly. Tying examples to characters from the story (Chinna, Kamala, the fruit seller) keeps the grammar grounded in familiar context.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (pp.17–18): circle the antonym of the highlighted word in each sentence.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'beautiful' on the board and asks students to call out its opposite. After taking responses, the teacher introduces the idea of antonyms — words that mean the opposite — and notes that all four target words in today's activity come directly from the story of Chinna.

Students read each of the four sentences in 'Let us Learn — C.' (pp.17–18) silently, identify the highlighted word, and predict the antonym before looking at the three options. They then circle the correct antonym and write one sentence of their own using the antonym.

The teacher discusses each item: for 'beautiful'→'ugly', 'reward'→'punishment', 'buy'→'sell', 'whispered'→'shouted', the teacher asks why the other options are wrong — e.g., why 'attractive' is a near-synonym of 'beautiful', not its opposite.
Students share one of their own sentences using an antonym from the task. The teacher selects two or three to write on the board and the class checks that the antonym is used correctly in context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may choose 'broken' for the opposite of 'beautiful' by associating broken objects with something unpleasant — clarify that 'ugly' is the semantic opposite, while 'broken' describes a physical state. The word 'whispered' appears in dialogue in the story (Chinna's request for chocolates), so linking back to that scene makes the antonym memorable.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.19–20): frame one sentence each for five words from the story.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the five story words on the board — smiling, mistake, honest, praise, careful — and asks students where each word appears in the story of Chinna. Students recall brief scenes, grounding each word in its narrative moment before writing begins.

The teacher models writing two sentences on the board: one for 'smiling' and one for 'honest', thinking aloud about choosing a subject and adding a meaningful detail ('Kamala was smiling when Chinna returned the money'). Students observe the model and note that the word must appear naturally in the sentence.

Students independently draft sentences for all five words in 'Let us Write — A.' (pp.19–20). The teacher circulates, nudging students who write only a fragment ('He is honest.') to add a context or reason ('He is honest because he gave back the extra money.').

Three or four students read their sentences aloud; the class gives a thumbs-up if the target word is used naturally and the sentence makes clear sense. The teacher praises variety — different subjects, different contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often frame very short sentences that are grammatically correct but semantically thin — 'She is careful.' — at this stage; use the story's scenes to prompt richer context, e.g., 'Be careful with the money, Chinna!' The five words span the story's main moral arc (smiling at the outcome, a mistake that was corrected, honesty, praise from the fruit seller, Kamala's caution), so drawing on that arc keeps writing grounded and purposeful.

periods.activity_title: Bell Craft: Making a Tinkling Bell

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.23): create a bell craft using recyclable materials, complete with decoration and a tag.

time_bands.activity: The teacher connects the craft to the story's central object — Chinna's joy at hearing the tinkling bells and tying them to Tara — and explains that students will make their own bell today. The step-by-step instructions are read aloud together.

Students work through the bell-making steps: filling a small tin or bottle cap with pebbles or beads, threading string, wrapping with foil, and decorating with markers or paint. The teacher circulates to assist with the hole punch or knot-tying steps that require care.

Students write their name or a short message on a small cardboard tag and attach it to their bell. Each student shakes the finished bell to test the tinkle, adjusting pebble count if the sound is too soft.

Students hold their bells up together and the teacher invites a brief sharing: 'If your bell were a gift for someone, who would it be for and why?' Two or three students share, connecting the craft back to Chinna's gift for Tara.

periods.teacher_notes: Collect recyclable materials (small bottle caps, tin lids, small pebbles or beads, foil, string, cardboard) before this unit — a small notice sent home the day prior, or a classroom collection point, works well. If hole-punch tools are unavailable, pre-punch the caps before the unit begins so students can focus on the threading and decoration steps.
materials: Small metal bottle caps or tin cans

periods.activity_title: Matchstick Puzzles and Bell Picture Collection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Matchsticks (p.23): move one matchstick to fix the equation shown in the puzzle.
Let us Explore (p.23): collect or draw pictures of different types of bells found in India.

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays or describes the solved matchstick example from p.23 — 9 − 2 = 8 corrected to 8 − 2 = 6 by moving one matchstick — and thinks aloud about which numeral could change with a single move. Students observe the logic before attempting the unsolved puzzle.

Students work individually or in pairs on the matchstick puzzle (p.23), drawing the numerals with matchstick strokes on paper and testing which stick to move. The teacher circulates, offering the prompt 'Which numeral could look like a different numeral with one stick moved?' for students who are stuck.

The teacher reveals and discusses the solution; students confirm or correct their answer. Brief class discussion: what kind of thinking helped — process of elimination, or spotting the numeral that looked 'almost right'?

Students begin the bell exploration task (p.23): they draw two or three types of bells found in India — temple bells, cowbells, school bells, door bells — and label each. Students who finish may add a sentence about where each bell is used.

periods.teacher_notes: Matchstick numerals can be unfamiliar to some students if they have not encountered seven-segment display style — briefly demonstrate how each digit (0–9) is made up of matchstick segments on the board before the puzzle begins. The bell-drawing task is open-ended; students who draw only one type of bell should be encouraged to think of bells in different settings — at home, at school, at a place of worship.
materials: Matchsticks or drawn matchstick diagrams on the board

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Honesty, Words, and Bells

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to retell the story of Chinna in four sentences — one for each key turning point: wanting the bells, losing the money, the honest return, and the reward. Two or three students share their retelling with the class, and together the class checks that all four turns are covered.

The teacher writes three sentences on the board using degrees of comparison and vocabulary from the chapter — e.g., 'Honesty is the best quality', 'Kamala is wiser than Chinna at that moment', 'Tara is the happiest animal on the farm' — and asks students to identify the comparison form and the antonym pair for one word in each sentence.

Students independently write three sentences of their own about the chapter: one that uses a comparative adjective, one that includes an antonym pair for a word from the story, and one that captures the chapter's central moral in their own words. The teacher circulates and gives brief individual feedback.
Students share their moral sentence with a partner, then the class votes on two or three sentences that best capture what the chapter taught. These are read aloud and appreciated by the group.

The teacher closes with an observational-curiosity prompt drawn from the chapter's wider world: 'Bells are used in many ways across India — in temples, on cattle, in schools, at festivals. What other sounds in your neighbourhood tell you something important is happening?' Students share two or three observations, connecting the story's tinkling bells to their own lived world.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on all the content threads of the chapter — the story's moral arc, the degrees of comparison grammar, the antonym vocabulary, the speaking dilemmas, and the world of bells — so any student, regardless of which earlier units their class experienced, can engage with at least one strand. The writing task is intentionally brief (three sentences) so that drafting, sharing, and reflection all happen within the unit's minutes.

items.source_context: Chinna's honesty, Kamala's guidance, the extra change, and Chacha's shop reward.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best explains why Kamala refused to let Chinna keep the extra ten rupees given by the fruit seller?

options.label: A
options.text: She reminded Chinna how sad he had felt when his own money went missing.

options.label: B
options.text: She thought Chinna already had enough money to buy the bells.

options.label: C
options.text: She wanted to save the money for buying fruits and vegetables.

options.label: D
options.text: She was angry that the fruit seller had made a mistake.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has confused Kamala's reason with a practical shopping concern rather than a moral lesson.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals the student focused on the error itself rather than on Kamala's empathy-based argument.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the student missed the detail that Chinna was relying on Kamala's promised money, not his own savings.

items.item_stem: After Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller, two things happened as a result. What were they? Write your answer in two sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The fruit seller was delighted and praised Chinna for his honesty. Kamala then took Chinna to Chacha's shop just before it closed, where he bought the tinkling bells for ten rupees.

items.item_stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads the following statements. Write T if the statement is true and F if it is false, based on what you hear.

options.text: Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller after his mother spoke to him.
Chinna went to Chacha's shop before going to the market with his mother.
The fruit seller was upset when Chinna gave back the ten rupees.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — F: Chinna visited Chacha's shop on the way home from school, before the market trip with his mother. 2 — T: After Kamala reminded Chinna how he had felt losing his own money, he ran back and returned the extra ten rupees. 3 — F: The fruit seller was delighted and praised Chinna for his honesty.
